summary: Defines a YANG data model for configuring and managing Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD), conforming to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342). It updates the earlier BFD YANG model from RFC 9127. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: BFD is a small protocol that watches a path and reports quickly when it breaks, so routing protocols can react faster. This RFC describes that protocol in YANG, the language network management software uses to read and write device configuration and state.

subtitle: A set of YANG modules for configuring BFD liveness sessions and reading their state, with an update to RFC 9127.

tldr.problem: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection runs over several kinds of paths, and each kind identifies its sessions differently. Operators need a standard way to configure BFD and read its state from management software.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a common BFD types module, a top-level module, and one module each for IP single-hop, IP multihop, LAG and MPLS LSP paths. All follow the Network Management Datastore Architecture, with configuration and state in the same tree.
tldr.outcome: It updates the model from RFC 9127. The main change is a new feature, client-base-cfg-parms, so BFD clients such as routing protocols can choose whether to carry per-session parameters.

sections.title: A YANG Model for BFD
sections.content:
This document defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) (RFC 5880). BFD is a network protocol used for liveness detection of arbitrary paths between systems. The paths it runs over include two systems directly connected via IP, which is known as BFD over single-hop IP and is also known as BFD for IPv4 and IPv6; two systems connected via multiple hops as described in RFC 5883; two systems connected via MPLS Label Switched Paths as described in RFC 5884; and two systems connected via a Link Aggregation Group interface as described in RFC 7130. Two systems connected via pseudowires, known as Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification, are described in RFC 5885 and are not addressed by this document.

BFD typically does not operate on its own. Various control protocols, also known as BFD clients, use the services it provides for their own operation, as described in RFC 5882. The obvious candidates are those that have no hellos to detect failures, such as static routes, and routing protocols whose hellos do not support sub-second failure detection, such as OSPF and IS-IS.

The YANG modules in this document conform to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342), which means the data models do not have separate top-level or sibling containers for configuration data and operational state data. This document updates the earlier model of the same name, RFC 9127. The change is a new feature, client-base-cfg-parms, together with an if-feature statement that conditionally includes definitions of parameters such as the multiplier or the desired minimum transmit interval. That lets implementations of protocols such as OSPF, IS-IS, PIM and BGP support both a model where those parameters are not needed, for instance when several BFD sessions share one interface, and a model where they are defined per session. As a result, the BFD MPLS module uses the base configuration parameters instead of the client ones, so that it can include all the parameters unconditionally.
sections.plainLanguage: Two features are named in the same way across the modules. The feature flag lets a vendor choose whether a routing protocol carries BFD timing values itself or leaves them to the BFD module, which is useful because some devices run several BFD sessions on one interface and cannot give each one its own timing.

sections.title: Why the Model Is Split into Several Modules
sections.content:
Since BFD is used for liveness detection of various forwarding paths, there is no uniform key to identify a BFD session. The BFD data model is therefore split into multiple YANG modules, where each module corresponds to one type of forwarding path. BFD for IP single-hop is in one module and BFD for MPLS in another. The main difference between these modules is how a BFD session is uniquely identified, that is, the key for the list containing the BFD sessions for that forwarding path. To avoid duplication of BFD definitions, common types and groupings are used by all the modules.

A new control plane protocol, bfdv1, is defined, and a bfd container is created under control-plane-protocol as specified in the routing management model of RFC 8349. That container is then augmented by four modules. The ietf-bfd-ip-sh module adds the ip-sh container for BFD sessions over IP single-hop. The ietf-bfd-ip-mh module adds the ip-mh container for BFD sessions over IP multihop. The ietf-bfd-lag module adds the lag container for BFD sessions over a LAG. The ietf-bfd-mpls module adds the mpls container for BFD over MPLS LSPs.

BFD can operate in three contexts: at the network-device level, in logical network elements as described in RFC 8530, and in network instances as described in RFC 8529. When used at the network-device level, the model is used as it stands. When used in a logical network element or a network instance, the BFD model augments the mounted routing model for that logical network element or network instance.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no single way to name a BFD session, because a session over a directly connected link is identified by the interface and the peer address, while a session over MPLS is identified by an address prefix. So the model is split: one module per kind of path, all sharing the same vocabulary, all hanging off one BFD container in the routing management tree.

sections.title: Common Configuration Parameters and Clients
sections.content:
The configuration model consists mainly of the parameters specified in BFD. Some implementations put BFD session configuration under the BFD clients, for example under routing applications such as OSPF, IS-IS or BGP, while others centralise it under BFD, outside the clients. The parameters of most interest to a BFD client are the multiplier and the intervals, because they determine how quickly the client converges when a failure occurs. Other parameters, such as BFD authentication, are not specific to the client's requirements, so configuration of BFD for all clients should be centralised.

That is a problem for clients that auto-discover their peers. IGPs do not have the peer address configured; the IGP is enabled on an interface and the peers are auto-discovered, so an operator would first have to determine the peer addresses, and would have to add configuration whenever a new peer appeared. To avoid this, the grouping client-cfg-parms is defined so that BFD clients can configure BFD, including the multiplier and intervals, for the sessions they need. When a new IGP peer is discovered, the IGP creates a BFD session to it, and when a peer goes away the IGP removes the session. How the sessions are created and removed is outside the scope of the document, but it would typically use an API implemented by the BFD module on the system. For clients that create sessions through their own configuration, authentication parameters are still specified in BFD.

The basic configuration parameters are the detection time multiplier local-multiplier, the desired minimum transmit interval desired-min-tx-interval, and the required minimum receive interval required-min-rx-interval. Although BFD allows different values for transmit and receive intervals, some implementations let the user specify one interval used for both. The model supports both, through the base-cfg-parms grouping, as a choice between min-interval and the separate transmit and receive values. For authentication, key-chain is a reference to the key chain model of RFC 8177, where the keys, algorithms and key lifetime are defined, and meticulous enables the meticulous mode of BFD.
sections.plainLanguage: The two numbers that matter most are how often to send a check and how many checks to miss before declaring the path down. The multiplier multiplies the interval to give the detection time, so three checks at one second means the path is declared down after about three seconds.

sections.title: One Module per Kind of Path
sections.content:
For single-hop IP, the ip-sh node holds a list of IP single-hop sessions, each uniquely identified by the interface and destination address pair. The node also holds a list of interfaces, used to specify authentication parameters for sessions that BFD clients create. Neither RFC 5880 nor RFC 5881 says whether the Echo function operates continuously or on demand, so the mechanism for starting and stopping it is implementation specific and is done by augmentation: configuration for a continuous Echo function, or an RPC for an on-demand one.

For multihop IP, because there are multiple paths, there can be multiple multihop sessions between a source and a destination address. That set is called a session group, and its key is the source address and the destination address. The module adds tx-ttl, the TTL of outgoing BFD control packets, and rx-ttl, the minimum TTL of incoming BFD control packets.

For MPLS Label Switched Paths, the document addresses LSPs whose Forwarding Equivalence Class is an IP address. The mpls node holds a list of sessions uniquely identified by an IP prefix, and again several sessions to one prefix form a session group. Because these LSPs are unidirectional, there is no LSP configuration on the egress node, but the BFD parameters for the egress node are added under mpls.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of path needs a different key, because the same peer can be reached over several equal-cost paths and each needs its own session. The multihop and MPLS modules therefore group the sessions under a source and destination pair, with the individual sessions inside.

sections.title: Operational State and Notifications
sections.content:
The operational state model contains both the overall statistics for the BFD sessions running on the device and the per-session operational information. The overall statistics, such as the number of BFD sessions and the number that are up, are available globally under the bfd node and also per type of forwarding path.

For each session, three categories of operational state data are shown. The first holds fundamental information about the session, such as the local discriminator, the remote discriminator, and whether Demand mode is supported. The second holds session-running information, such as the remote BFD state and the diagnostic code received, the actual transmit interval between control packets, which may differ from the configured desired minimum transmit interval, the actual receive interval, and the actual transmit interval between Echo packets. The third holds the detailed statistics for the session, such as when the session last changed state and how long it has been in that state.

For some path types there may be more than one session on the virtual path to the destination. With IP multihop and MPLS LSPs there can be multiple BFD sessions from the source to the same destination, testing the various equal-cost paths. This is represented by having multiple sessions under each session-group.

The model defines notifications to inform end users of important events detected during protocol operation. The local discriminator identifies the corresponding BFD session on the local system and the remote discriminator identifies it on the remote system. Notifications also give more important details about sessions, such as the new state, the time in the previous state, the network instance, and the reason the state changed. Notifications are defined for each type of forwarding path but reuse groupings for the common information. The document defines no RPC operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The state tree tells you what each session is doing right now: whether it is up, what the peer reported, and when it last changed. The notifications are the same information pushed as events when something happens, so a management system does not have to poll.

sections.title: Example Configurations
sections.content:
The document gives worked examples for each of the four path types it covers. The IP single-hop example shows a session configured on an interface towards a destination address, with the common configuration parameters. The IP multihop example shows a session group keyed by source and destination address, with the transmit and receive TTLs that control how far the BFD packets travel. The LAG example shows a session over a link aggregation group, including the per-member-link detail that the LAG case needs. The MPLS example shows a session group for an address prefix, with the egress-side parameters for the node that terminates the label switched path.

Appendix A gives an example YANG module for configuring the Echo function, which Section 2.1.2 leaves to implementations because the base BFD specifications do not say whether it runs continuously or on demand.
sections.plainLanguage: Each example shows the same handful of settings placed under a different key, because that is what changes between the path types. The Echo function example shows how an implementation might add the on-demand control without changing the base model.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The YANG modules define schemas for data designed to be accessed with network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, where the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is Secure Shell, and the lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, where the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model provides the means to restrict access for particular users to a preconfigured subset of the available operations and content.

A number of data nodes are writable, creatable or deletable, and may be considered sensitive. Write operations on these nodes without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. For the single-hop, multihop and LAG session lists, the multiplier and interval nodes affect the session, and the source and destination address nodes can be used to send BFD packets to unwitting recipients, a threat RFC 5880 describes how BFD mitigates. The authentication nodes key-chain and meticulous affect the security of the session. The system should police the creation of BFD sessions so that new ones do not cause existing sessions to fail, and the BFD protocol has mechanisms that allow in-service modification.

Some readable nodes are also sensitive. The summary counters disclose how many sessions are up, down or admin-down, and they include sessions the reader has no access to. Access to the local and remote discriminator data nodes, combined with the data nodes in the authentication container, provides the ability to spoof BFD packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risks are that someone changes the timing values to make the network flap, or reads the discriminators and uses them to forge BFD packets. The access control model is what stops both, so write access to the session lists has to be restricted.
